name: Propositum
description: Watches the sources you approve, while a work session is running. Nothing else.
_comment_permissions: WAS: 'Every permission here is WARNING-FREE at install. Chrome shows no
scary prompt for any of them, which matters because a consumer product
that asks to read your browsing history has already lost the argument it
is trying to make.'
SUPERSEDED 2026-08-17 by ADR-0013, which adds tabGroups and pays one
warning for it. The sentiment survives and the sentence does not: what
matters is that a permission the person is warned about is one somebody
argued for in writing, not that the count of warnings is zero. See
_comment_tabgroups below for the argument, the price, and the mechanism
that keeps it narrower than the warning implies.
SAID, THE SAME DAY: 'The rest of this list is still warning-free.' FALSE,
and corrected 2026-08-17 against Chrome's permissions reference
(https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/permissions-list).
Two of the seven entries below show a string of their own:
notifications  'Display notifications.'
debugger       'Access the page debugger backend.' AND 'Read and change
all your data on all websites.' The first is its own
string and is NOT the host warning restated.
Warning-free, all five of them: alarms, idle, scripting, sidePanel,
storage. So the opening sentence had already been false since debugger
landed, and tests/capture.test.ts has counted debugger as not-warning-free
since that day. tabGroups makes three strings, not one.
CORRECTED 2026-08-17 (ADR-0008; docs/research/intent-signals.md 2.1 and
4.1). Two of the three reasons below were wrong, and both are left in place
struck rather than deleted, because what they claimed is what a reader of
this file has believed since ADR-0002.
DELIBERATELY ABSENT — see ADR-0002:
tabs          would grant the URL and title of EVERY tab. WAS: 'without it
the extension is structurally incapable of learning the
person visited anything they did not approve; Chrome
enforces the constraint, not our code.' FALSE since
2026-08-11. chrome.tabs.query() needs no permission at all —
the permission only unscrubs url, pendingUrl, title and
favIconUrl on what comes back, and host_permissions
['https://*/*'] unscrubs them too. One line in
service-worker.js would return every open https tab today.
No line is that line. STILL ABSENT, and what holds it is
tests/extension-permissions.test.ts, which is our code
remembering — see docs/SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY.md, 'Data
explicitly not collected'.
webNavigation WAS: 'costs the Read your browsing history warning'. FALSE
since 2026-08-11. Under https://*/* Chrome's first host rule
absorbs kTab, kWebNavigation, kTopSites and kFavicon, so
adding this adds NO string to the install prompt and would
not even disable the extension pending re-approval. What is
still true is the part that was never the reason: it carries
transitionType — the most semantically loaded signal there
is ('typed it' vs 'followed a link'). We give it up and take
document.referrer plus Navigation Timing as partial
substitutes. The exclusion now stands on capability, and
ADR-0008 says what would have to be argued to take it.
history       not needed and not defensible. This one is unchanged: its
warning is NOT absorbed, and it is the one consumers know.
WAS: 'notifications is warning-free and is the ONLY way to surface an
offer nobody asked for.' The first half is FALSE and was corrected
2026-08-17: Chrome's permissions reference gives notifications the warning
'Display notifications.' It is a mild string and it is still a string. The
second half stands and is the reason the permission is here:
sidePanel.open() requires a user gesture, so calling it from an alarm
silently throws — which is exactly what happened: the app named the
subject correctly and the person saw nothing but a small dot.
_comment_tabgroups: SAID HERE FIRST, AND WRONG: 'The FIRST permission in this manifest that is
not warning-free.' Corrected the same day against Chrome's permissions
reference: notifications and debugger each show a string already, so this
is the THIRD. What is true, and is what the decision rested on, is that it
is the first permission taken for a CAPTURE SIGNAL that shows a string of
its own — the others buy mechanisms — and that its string is not absorbed
by host_permissions.
The opening sentence of the block above ('Every permission here is
WARNING-FREE at install') stops being defensible today, and had in fact
been false since debugger landed. It is struck up there rather than
quietly edited, because what a reader of this file has believed since
ADR-0002 is worth leaving on the page beside what replaced it.
THE PRICE, IN CHROME'S OWN WORDS: 'View and manage your tab groups.'
It is NOT absorbed by host_permissions ['https://*/*'] the way tabs,
webNavigation, topSites and favicon are — see docs/research/intent-signals.md
4.1 — so this one is shown to the person at install, and adding it in an
update DOES disable the extension pending re-approval. That is the correct
shape for a new capability and is not a reason to avoid it.
WHAT IT GRANTS: chrome.tabGroups. That is group METADATA — id, title,
color, collapsed, windowId — and nothing else.
WHAT IT DOES NOT GRANT, and this is the whole argument: the tabs inside a
group. Chrome's own reference: 'To group and ungroup tabs, or to query
what tabs are in groups, use the chrome.tabs API.' We hold no tabs
permission and call no chrome.tabs.query — both still forbidden by
tests/extension-permissions.test.ts, unchanged, in the same diff that adds
this line.
WHAT KEEPS IT NARROW, mechanically: the only group id this extension ever
looks up comes from sender.tab.groupId on a message sent by a content
script we ALREADY have permission to run — see groupTitleOf in
service-worker.js. So the set of groups it can see is the set of groups
containing a page it was already watching. There is deliberately no call to
chrome.tabGroups.query, which would enumerate every group in every window
and is a different capability nobody has argued for; the permission grants
it and this extension declines it, which is the same behavioural-rather-
than-structural guarantee the tabs entry above now rests on.
WHY IT IS WORTH THE WARNING: docs/research/intent-signals.md 4.3. A tab
group title is a name the person typed for their own thread of work. It is
the sentence src/domain/detection/topics.ts spends 850 lines reconstructing
by string arithmetic and a model call. It may only ever improve a NAME:
tests/detection.test.ts pins that grounds and sufficiency are byte-identical
with and without one, so it cannot make an offer fire that would not have.
WHAT IT IS, FOR THE PRIVACY DOCUMENT: person-authored text, arriving on the
ambient path, bounded at 120 characters, held in the same in-memory buffer
under the same window and row cap, discarded on decline. It is not page
text and it is not a tab list. It IS the first thing Propositum captures
that the PERSON wrote rather than a page — which is a category worth naming
rather than filing under 'metadata'.
_comment_debugger: REVERSAL. ADR-0002 listed `debugger` under 'explicitly NOT', with the
reason 'would make every constraint below advisory'. That was correct.
ADR-0010 grants it anyway, and the price is stated in that ADR's opening
paragraph rather than buried: it is the first decision in this series
whose net effect on safety is negative.
It is here because every job people actually want done — reply in this
thread, fill this form, pull my orders out of this account — lives behind
a session Propositum's own browser does not have and must not be given.
The alternative was copying a credential out of Chrome, which is worse in
every dimension: invisible to the person, revocable only by changing a
password, and it turns a bounded local mistake into a durable one.
What holds the line now that the permission is granted:
- The tab is one Propositum OPENED. chrome.debugger.getTargets is never
called, chrome.tabs.query and chrome.tabs.get are never called, and
chrome.tabs.create is the only source of a tab id in this extension.
CORRECTED 2026-08-17: this bullet used to end 'that constraint is still
enforced by Chrome refusing rather than by our code remembering, which
is the one place ADR-0002's original argument survives intact.' That
was false. tabs.query needs no permission, so nothing is being refused
— the four calls above are absent because nobody wrote them, and
tests/extension-permissions.test.ts is what keeps them absent. See the
tabs entry above and ADR-0010 section 1, both amended the same day.
- No Runtime domain, ever. Propositum never runs a line of its own
JavaScript inside a page the person is signed into. Clicks are
synthesised at coordinates; see extension/src/cdp.js.
- Chrome's own attachment bar is unsuppressible and its Cancel is a free
kill switch. src/overlay.js adds the layer Chrome's bar cannot: which
tab, in plain language, with a Stop.
- tests/extension-cdp.test.ts greps this extension for the calls that
must never appear. The extension has no build step, so the file under
review is the file Chrome runs and a grep is a real guard.
_comment_hosts: BROAD BY DECISION, and this reverses ADR-0002. Detection cannot work on
sources the person has not set up yet, and the whole point of the feature
is noticing work before they have told us about it. That costs Chrome's
'Read and change all your data on all websites' warning at install, which
is the honest price and is not hidden anywhere in the UI.
What limits the exposure is NOT the permission any more, so it has to be
the behaviour, and it is enforced in two places:
- content.js sends METADATA ONLY while no session is running: a cleaned
URL, a title, dwell, scroll, how the page was left, and — where the
person made one — the title of the tab group the page sits in. Never
page text.
(2026-08-17, FIRST NOTE, now superseded: 'true of content.js and NOT of
what the app receives on the ambient path. flushAmbient in
service-worker.js rebuilds the wire shape field by field and omits
scrollFraction, so no scroll leaves the browser while no session is
running. ADR-0008's capture row says why that line has not simply been
added.')
(2026-08-17, SECOND NOTE — ADR-0013, now superseded in its last
sentence only: the missing line was added, along with exitType and
groupTitle, so all four now leave the browser. Scroll is copied only
when it is already within [0,1] — omitting an out-of-range reading is
what every reading got until today, so which batches the app accepts
did not change. 'Nothing in the detector reads scroll or exit type even
now; tests/reachability.test.ts holds both as deferred assertions so
wiring one cannot happen quietly.')
(2026-08-20, THIRD NOTE — ADR-0018: the quoted sentence above is false
in both halves. The detector reads both — grounds.ts refuses a page
nobody scrolled that was switched away from, and requires half a page
on each of three sites before it calls an afternoon comparison
shopping — and the deferred assertions that were said to guard this no
longer exist. Nothing about what this file grants changed; what changed
is that these two signals now move whether Propositum offers at all,
which is a thing a person reading this manifest should be told.)
- the app holds those in memory, bounded and discarded, and they never
reach the ledger unless the person accepts an offer.
Full page text still begins only after a session starts on an approved
source, exactly as before.
_comment_loopback: The app's own origin, and the ONLY entry here that is not warning-free.
A service worker fetch to http://127.0.0.1 is cross-origin, and the app
sends no CORS headers deliberately — CORS protects nothing on loopback,
which is why the transport has four controls of its own. Without this the
extension cannot reach the app at all: the health check fails, the badge
shows '!', and capture is silently OFF.
Pinned to the port in package.json's dev script; a test asserts they match.
_comment_key: Pinned so the extension id is stable. Without it the id changes if the repo
moves, and the Origin check on the loopback transport starts rejecting our
~~REPLACE before any real install — this is a placeholder.~~ PINNED
2026-09-03, on the owner's say-so. The id derived from the key below is
oeeehaokemppjoedlccgggmhlmhcdeln — sha256 of the DER public key, first
128 bits, hex digits mapped a-p — and tests/extension-permissions.test.ts
recomputes it from this file so the two cannot drift. The private half
lives outside the repository, with the owner, and is needed only to pack
a .crx; nothing in the product reads it. Changing this key mints a new id
and orphans every install that exists, including the development pairing
on the machine it was pinned from — that is why it was left for the owner
and why it is not to be regenerated.
